title: Average rate of change as a difference quotient
ced_evidence: CHA-2.A.1: The difference quotients f(a+h)-f(a)/h and f(x)-f(a)/(x-a) express the average rate of change of a function over an interval.

title: Derivative at a point: two equivalent limit forms
ced_evidence: CHA-2.B.1: The instantaneous rate of change of a function at x = a ... provided the limit exists. These are equivalent forms of the definition of the derivative

title: Derivative of f as a function
ced_evidence: CHA-2.B.2: The derivative of f is the function whose value at x is lim h→0 [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h, provided this limit exists.

title: Derivative notations for y = f(x)
body: The CED names three notations for the derivative of y = f(x).

items.label: dy/dx
items.meaning: Leibniz notation for the derivative of y with respect to x

items.label: f'(x)
items.meaning: Function notation for the derivative of f

items.label: y'
items.meaning: Prime notation for the derivative of y

caution: If you introduce a new name for a derivative expression, define it. Do not silently rename it.
ced_evidence: CHA-2.B.3: For y = f(x), notations for the derivative include dy/dx, f′(x), and y′.

title: Representations of the derivative
body: The derivative can be represented in four ways.

items.label: Graphical
items.meaning: Slope of the tangent line on the graph; the graph of f' is not the graph of f

items.label: Numerical
items.meaning: Values in a table, e.g. estimated from difference quotients

items.label: Verbal
items.meaning: A description of an instantaneous rate of change

ced_evidence: CHA-2.B.4: The derivative can be represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally.

title: Tangent line at x = a
ced_evidence: CHA-2.C and CHA-2.C.1: The derivative of a function at a point is the slope of the line tangent to a graph of the function at that point.

title: Keep notation precise: parentheses and defined names
body: Keep parentheses around grouped factors and do not drop notation, since procedural errors in notation cost points even when the calculus is right.
ced_evidence: Building the Mathematical Practices: students may drop important notation, such as a parenthesis

title: Estimating a derivative from a table (difference quotient)
caution: Write the difference quotient itself. A correct number without this structure can lose the point.

title: Calculator answers: rounding
body: Present the expression evaluated on the calculator and round or truncate to three places after the decimal point.
ced_evidence: CHA-2.D.2; Preparing for the AP Exam: rounding or truncating to three places after the decimal point

title: Differentiable implies continuous (not the converse)
body: If a function is differentiable at a point, it is continuous there, but a continuous function may fail to be differentiable at a point in its domain.
caution: If a point is not in the domain of f, it is not in the domain of f'.
ced_evidence: FUN-2.A.1: If a function is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.; FUN-2.A.2: A continuous function may fail to be differentiable at a point in its domain.

title: How a continuous function can fail to be differentiable
body: CED illustrative examples of non-differentiability at a point in the domain.

items.label: Unequal one-sided limits
items.meaning: The left and right limits of the difference quotient are not equal, as in f(x)=|x| at x=0

items.label: Vertical tangent
items.meaning: The tangent line is vertical and has no slope, as in f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x} at x=0

ced_evidence: FUN-2.A.2 illustrative examples: The left hand and right hand limits of the difference quotient are not equal; The tangent line is vertical and has no slope

title: Power rule
ced_evidence: FUN-3.A.1: derivative for functions of the form f(x) = x^r

title: Constant, constant multiple, sum and difference rules
ced_evidence: FUN-3.A.2: Sums, differences, and constant multiples of functions can be differentiated using derivative rules.; FUN-3.A.3 (polynomials)

title: Derivatives of sin x, cos x, e^x, ln x
ced_evidence: FUN-3.A.4: Specific rules can be used to find the derivatives for sine, cosine, exponential, and logarithmic functions.

title: Evaluate a limit by recognizing a derivative
body: If a limit has the form of the definition of the derivative of a function whose derivative is known, evaluate the limit by finding that derivative.
ced_evidence: LIM-3.A.1: recognizing an expression for the definition of the derivative of a function whose derivative is known offers a strategy for determining a limit.

title: Product rule
caution: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. Show the rule's structure, e.g. f'(3)=u(3)v'(3)+v(3)u'(3), then substitute values.
ced_evidence: FUN-3.B.1: Derivatives of products of differentiable functions can be found using the product rule.

title: Quotient rule
ced_evidence: FUN-3.B.2: Derivatives of quotients of differentiable functions can be found using the quotient rule.

title: Rewriting tan, cot, sec, csc with identities
body: \tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x},\quad \cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x},\quad \sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x},\quad \csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}
ced_evidence: FUN-3.B.3: Rearranging tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant functions using identities allows differentiation using derivative rules.

title: Derivatives of tan, cot, sec, csc
body: \frac{d}{dx}[\tan x]=\sec^{2}x,\quad \frac{d}{dx}[\cot x]=-\csc^{2}x,\quad \frac{d}{dx}[\sec x]=\sec x\tan x,\quad \frac{d}{dx}[\csc x]=-\csc x\cot x
ced_evidence: FUN-3.B.3 (Topic 2.10: Finding the Derivatives of Tangent, Cotangent, Secant, and/or Cosecant Functions)
